This first petition has been filed under Section 483 of Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 for grant of Regular Bail to the petitioner in case bearing FIR No.421 dated 10.7.2020 under Sections 307, 386, 120- B 201 IPC, 1860 and Section 25 of Arms Act, 1959 registered at Police Station Model Town, District Rewari.
2. FIR in the present case was registered on the statement of Vikash Yadav.

The same reads thus:-
"Stated that am resident of above said address.
Earlier I used to do business of finance and now working as Commission Agent (Aadhti).
Before Lockdown, Chand Mundanwas had called me and told me that his men are incarcerated and also told me expenditure which to is give their about 1-15 lacs, upon which I refused.
After this shots were fired upon Bir Singh, 1 of 5 214 CRM-M-4631-2026 (O&M) resident of Mundanwas and Tillu on separate occasions.
At that time I had received intimation from my friends that Vikash, you also be aware, but I ignored it.
Today, I was sitting at my vend in Vegetable Market, Bithwana, at that time at about 7.10 AM three young boys came there and fired upon me with intention to kill.

After this I had received two gunshot wound at the back of my head and one gunshot wound on my right shoulder,
due to which I fell down and they fled towards the road.
Chand resident of Mundanwas by hatching a conspiracy with his companions have got fired gunshot upon me with an intention to kill.
They by getting firing conducted in public want to make a big name in Rewari.
Vikash son Satpal, resident of of Rewari was sitting along with me, who is my partner.

sentences.text: 3. Learned Senior counsel for the petitioner contends that the petitioner was arrested in the present case on 21.12.2021 and since then he has been in custody.
He contends that initially three persons namely Aman, Mahipal and the petitioner herein were nominated as an accused.
Learned counsel further submits that the other two co-accused, Aman and Mahipal, have already been granted the concession of regular bail.
It is argued that, considering the long period of custody already undergone by the petitioner and applying the principle of parity, the petitioner is entitled to similar relief.

It is argued with vehemence that the case of the petitioner, in any case, is at a better footing as compared to the other co-accused, who have already been granted the concession of regular bail in the year 2024 inasmuch as two witnesses 2 of 5 214 CRM-M-4631-2026 (O&M) participated in the Test Identification Parade (TIP) qua the co-accused, whereas no such TIP was ever conducted in respect of the petitioner.
4. Learned State however counsel contends that out of total 50 prosecution witnesses, 31 have already been examined and now the case is fixed for prosecution evidence for 24.03.2026.
She contends that the petitioner is involved in multiple heinous offences and that his release on bail is likely to adversely influence the prosecution witnesses.

She submits that the prosecution shall make every endeavor to conclude the prosecution evidence expeditiously in any case within a period of 03 months from the date next fixed before the trial Court for recording of prosecution evidence.
5. I have heard the learned counsel for the respective parties and have gone through the documents appended with the present petition with their able assistance.

6. Although the period of custody already undergone by the petitioner does inspire some equities in his favour, however, the nature and material of the cases registered against him dissuade this Court from extending the benefit of bail.

7. It is evident from a perusal of the above that there are as many as 04 cases under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 that have been registered against the petitioner, each at a different jurisdiction i.e. at Meham in Rohtak (Haryana), at P.S. Sadar Malout, Sri Muktsar Sahib (Punjab), at Kotkasim (Rajasthan) and at Kasola in Rewari (Haryana).

Additionally, the petitioner is also facing prosecution in as many as 05 cases for commission of offences under Section 307 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 apart from other offences and significantly, these offences have likewise been registered across distinct jurisdictions.

The involvement of the petitioner in a large number of heinous offences reflects a persistent pattern of criminal conduct, indicating that the petitioner has seemingly chosen 4 of 5 214 CRM-M-4631-2026 (O&M) crime as a means of livelihood.

In such circumstances, the release of the petitioner on bail is likely to adversely impact the prosecution case,
including the possibility of influencing, intimidating or dissuading prosecution witnesses.
Consequently, the present petition for seeking regular bail to the petitioner is dismissed at this stage.
The trial Court is directed to make an endeavor for expeditious conclusion of the remaining prosecution evidence and preferably within a period of 03 months from the date next fixed before it.
